archetype.name: Better Than Its Record (pass-first)
archetype.definition: A Houston team whose efficiency and point differential belong to a roughly .500 club, but whose record has been dragged down by close losses, a defense that gives up big plays, and a run game that can't carry its share.

report.headline: A .500 team wearing a 2-5 record; the close losses won't keep breaking this way.
report.take:
Houston has quietly flipped identities. The last three seasons were built on defense, and the 2025 unit ranked 2nd in EPA allowed on the way to 12 wins. This year the offense is the steadier half. C.J. Stroud has started every game behind a line that ranks 6th in pressure rate allowed, and the pass offense sits 12th in EPA per play. Meanwhile the defense has slid to 24th in EPA allowed.

The record is the misleading part. Houston has been outscored by just 5 points, and its differential implies 4.2 wins, not two. That gap is why the Texans rank 31st in wins over expected. Every loss except the Cincinnati game came by one score, including shootouts with Buffalo and Dallas and a 17-19 loss at Indianapolis. They have won only 0.2 of their one-score games. Turnovers aren't the culprit either: the margin is positive, 11th in the league. This is a team losing coin flips, and coin flips tend to even out.

The raw numbers do hide real flaws, and they explain why those close games tip the wrong way. The defense wins most snaps. It ranks 7th in success rate allowed and has 21 sacks, 2nd in the league. But it gives up explosive passes at the highest rate in the league and ranks 26th on deep throws. Red-zone defense (23rd) turns those chunk gains into touchdowns. On offense, the run game is a dead end: 3.3 yards a carry and 25th in rush EPA, behind a line that loses at the point of attack and draws flags (28th in line penalties). The team commits 8.3 penalties a game. A team that can't run, drives itself backward and allows big plays will lose a lot of close games.

Where it goes from here depends on whether the explosive-play problem is structural or noise. Big plays allowed are usually less stable than down-to-down success, and this staff's recent history is strong defense. Expect the results to drift toward the underlying profile. That points to a winning record the rest of the way, but the 2-5 hole and Jacksonville's 5-2 start make the division a long shot.

strengths.title: Clean pocket, efficient Stroud passing
strengths.body: The line has been far better in protection than in the run game: 6th in pressure rate allowed and 6th in QB hit rate allowed. That has let Stroud post a top-12 pass EPA despite a target tree spread across a tight end and several receivers. Pass protection held up even against Jacksonville's top-3 defense, with zero sacks allowed. With the same starter all year, this is the most bankable part of the team.

strengths.title: Elite sack production up front
strengths.body: Only one team has more sacks, and Houston ranks 5th in sack rate. It ranks only 10th in pressure rate, so the rush finishes at an unusually high clip. Some of that finishing rate may cool, but the pressure is real. That drives the strong down-to-down defense: 7th in success rate allowed.

strengths.title: Point differential says .500
strengths.body: A -5 point differential and 4.2 implied wins put this team near the middle of the league, not near the bottom. The record gap comes from close-game results rather than turnover luck: the giveaway margin is actually positive. Close-game records tend to regress toward even.

concerns.title: Defense bleeds explosive passes
concerns.body: The defense wins most snaps but allows explosive passes at the worst rate in the league and ranks 26th on deep throws. When it does break, the red-zone defense (23rd) rarely saves it. Both starting safeties are questionable, which makes this harder to fix in the short term. History suggests the scheme is better than this, but it is the main reason close games are slipping.

concerns.title: No run game to close games
concerns.body: At 3.3 yards a carry with 2.16 yards before contact, the backs are getting hit early. The line, not the backs, is the root cause, and it is unlikely to change mid-season. That leaves Houston unable to protect leads or grind out short yardage, and puts the full weight on Stroud. With David Montgomery questionable, Woody Marks carries most of the load.

concerns.title: Penalties and a soft run defense
concerns.body: At 8.3 penalties a game (26th), with 508 penalty yards, drives stall and opponents get second chances. The run defense ranks 29th in EPA allowed and gave up 188 rushing yards to the Giants in a loss as a 10-point favorite. Flag discipline is fixable. A run defense that soft is a matchup issue opponents will keep testing.

trend.note: The pass offense has swung wildly: deeply negative against Cincinnati and Indianapolis, then three strong weeks capped by a win in Jacksonville. Then came a flat home loss to the Giants, in which the run defense was gashed. The baseline is solid, but week-to-week variance is high.

nextGame.headline: Rested Houston's pass rush meets the league's worst protection
nextGame.body:
Houston comes off two weeks of rest to face a winless Chargers team that ranks last in offensive EPA and last in pass EPA. The core matchup is lopsided: the league's No. 2 sack defense against a line ranked 31st in sack rate and last in QB hit rate allowed. The catch is that the Chargers' defense is legitimate, 8th in pass EPA allowed, 6th on third down and 10th in the red zone. Los Angeles leans on the run harder than anyone (last in pass rate over expected), which aims straight at Houston's softest spot. The Book has Houston -4.5 with a 40.5 total, which points to a grinding, lower-scoring game.

Availability tilts toward Houston. The Chargers' secondary is thin: Derwin James is on IR, and corners Donte Jackson, Deane Leonard and Rodney Shelley are all listed out. Guard Kayode Awosika is out on a line that already can't protect, while tight end David Njoku may be nearing a return. For Houston, both starting safeties, Jalen Pitre and Reed Blankenship, are questionable, which matters for a defense that gives up big plays. Montgomery's groin leaves the backfield to Marks if he sits, and Jaylin Noel is out for the year.

waysToWin.title: Pass rush wrecks the Chargers' protection
waysToWin.body: Houston's sack rate ranks 5th, and Los Angeles allows sacks at the 31st-ranked rate behind a line missing a guard. Pressure that forces the Chargers out of their run-first plan puts their bottom-ranked passing game in long-yardage spots. This is the clearest edge on the field.

waysToWin.title: Stroud attacks a depleted secondary
waysToWin.body: The Chargers' pass defense has played well, but with James on IR and three corners out, the depth behind it is being tested. Houston's protection should give Stroud time. The Chargers' WR2 has outscored his usual production against them, which favors a spread-out target tree like Houston's.

waysToWin.title: Win the hidden-yardage game
waysToWin.body: Los Angeles sits 30th in turnover margin and 31st in penalties per game, and its offense can't sustain drives when it falls behind schedule. If Houston keeps its own flags in check, the field-position edge should turn into a multi-score lead.

waysToLose.title: Chargers' ground game repeats Giants script
waysToLose.body: Los Angeles runs more than any offense relative to expectation, and Houston ranks 29th in rush EPA allowed. The Chargers' run game is poor on its own (31st in rush EPA), but the Giants showed that this defense can be bullied. A ball-control game keeps the score low and close.

waysToLose.title: Drives die against a good defense
waysToLose.body: Houston can't run, and the Chargers' defense is stingy on third down and in the red zone. Field goals instead of touchdowns keep a winless team in a one-score game, where Houston has won only 0.2 of its chances. The Chargers also have 10 takeaways, 8th in the league, so stalled drives can turn into short fields.

waysToLose.title: One shot play beats thin safeties
waysToLose.body: Houston gives up explosive passes at the league's worst rate, and both starting safeties are questionable. Even a bottom-ranked passing offense can flip a low-total game with a couple of deep completions. Add Houston's usual flags extending drives, and an upset becomes plausible.

nextGame.watch: Whether Houston's rush gets home early on passing downs. If the Chargers' line can't hold up, a run-first plan with no passing fallback collapses.

restOfSeason.body:
The underlying profile is a middle-of-the-pack team that has lost most of its close games. Expect a better record from here: the pass offense and protection are stable with the same quarterback, and the down-to-down defense is good. The worst-in-the-league explosive-pass rate should ease if the safeties get healthy, given this staff's track record on defense. Neither the run game nor the run defense shows signs of a quick fix. That keeps Houston in close games, so the record will stay sensitive to late-game coin flips.

The schedule is mixed. Indianapolis, Tennessee, Philadelphia and Washington are all winnable. Pittsburgh, Green Bay, Cleveland and a Jacksonville team ranked 3rd on both sides of the ball are real tests, many of them on the road. A finish around .500 is the most likely outcome. That is enough to make the record respectable, but a three-game deficit to Jacksonville leaves a division title an outside chance.
swingFactors: Safeties' health and the explosive-pass rate
Run defense against physical, run-heavy opponents

confidence.note: Seven games with a stable QB, but close-game swings and a defensive drop-off make the read on the defense uncertain.
